# The story

## The dean's sleep report {.center}

The dean wants a one-page summary of the sleep survey:

1. **How much** do students in each program sleep? (**Numbers**, Chapter 13)
2. **When** do they go to bed? (**Strings**, Chapter 14)
3. Can we make the chart **readable**? (**Factors**, Chapter 16)

::: {.notes}
~3 min. Show the finished chart on the next slide, then tell them they will be able to build it by the end of the lecture.
:::

## Where we are going

```{webr}
#| context: setup
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

survey <- read_csv("data/sleep_survey_v2.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| context: output
#| autorun: true
survey |>
  filter(!is.na(sleep_hours)) |>
  group_by(program) |>
  summarize(mean_sleep = mean(sleep_hours)) |>
  mutate(
    hours = mean_sleep %/% 1,
    minutes = round((mean_sleep %% 1) * 60),
    program = fct_reorder(program, mean_sleep),
    label = str_glue("{hours} h {minutes} min")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_sleep, y = program)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), nudge_y = 0.3) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(5, 8)) +
  labs(
    title = "Average sleep by program",
    x = "Hours per night", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

- Programs are **ordered** by how much they sleep
- Each point has a readable **label**
- The averages are **rounded** and split into hours and minutes

## Setup and data

The data is the same sleep survey from Lecture 8. It is loaded once at the start:

```r
library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(tibble); library(readr)
library(ggplot2); library(stringr); library(forcats)

survey <- read_csv("data/sleep_survey_v2.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
glimpse(survey)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Not everything fits in 80 minutes"}
Some tools are in the **appendix tables** at the end. Each row says what the tool does and which section of the chapter to read.
:::


# Part 1: Numbers

::: {.notes}
~25 min including Exercise 1.
:::

## How much do students sleep?

Our goal for this part: one row per program, with the average sleep, nicely rounded.

| Step | Tool (Chapter 13) |
|------|-------------------|
| Count students | `count()`, `n()`, `n_distinct()` |
| Fix numbers typed as text | `parse_number()` |
| Transform columns | `pmin()`, `pmax()`, `%/%`, `%%`, `round()`, `cut()` |
| Rank programs | `min_rank()` |
| Summarize | `mean()`, `median()`, `sd()`, `IQR()` |

## Making numbers: `parse_double()`

Numbers sometimes arrive as text, typically when data is imported. readr has two parsers:

- `parse_double()` for strings that are clean numbers
- `parse_number()` for strings that have extra text around the number

```{webr}
x <- c("1.2", "5.6", "1e3")
parse_double(x)
```

## `parse_number()`

`parse_number()` ignores text before and after the number. That makes it handy for currency, percentages, and similar messy values.

```{webr}
x <- c("$1,234", "USD 3,513", "59%")
parse_number(x)
```

Imagine students had typed their weekly work hours as text:

```{webr}
work <- c("10 hours", "12h", "about 8")
parse_number(work)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Grouping marks too"}
The comma in `$1,234` is handled. The result is the number 1234.
:::

## Counting with `count()`

Much of data science is counting. dplyr's `count()` gives a quick tally of how many rows have each value.

```{webr}
survey |> count(program)
```

Add `sort = TRUE` to see the biggest groups first:

```{webr}
survey |> count(favourite_drink, sort = TRUE)
```

- Notice the `NA` row: those are students who left the drink blank

## The long way

`count()` is a shortcut. Building it by hand lets you compute extra summaries in the same step.

```{webr}
survey |>
  group_by(program) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean_sleep = mean(sleep_hours, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

::: {.callout-warning title="n() only works inside dplyr verbs"}
`n()` takes no arguments and returns the size of the current group. Outside of `summarize()`, `mutate()`, or `filter()`, there is no "current group", so it fails.
:::

```{webr}
#| error: true
n()
```

## `n_distinct()`

`n_distinct(x)` counts the **unique** values of `x`. A quick check: does every student appear only once?

```{webr}
survey |>
  summarize(
    students = n(),
    unique_ids = n_distinct(student_id)
  )
```

How many different drinks does each program have?

```{webr}
survey |>
  group_by(program) |>
  summarize(
    with_na = n_distinct(favourite_drink),
    without_na = n_distinct(favourite_drink, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

::: {.callout-caution title="NA counts as a value"}
By default `n_distinct()` counts `NA` as one more distinct value. Add `na.rm = TRUE` if you do not want that.
:::

## Weighted counts

A weighted count is a sum. For example, the total weekly study hours in each program:

```{webr}
survey |>
  group_by(program) |>
  summarize(total_study = sum(study_hours_week))
```

`count()` has a `wt` argument that does the same thing:

```{webr}
survey |> count(program, wt = study_hours_week)
```

## Counting missing values

Combine `sum()` with `is.na()` (recall from Lecture 8 that `TRUE` counts as 1). How many students in each program left `sleep_hours` blank?

```{webr}
survey |>
  group_by(program) |>
  summarize(n_blank = sum(is.na(sleep_hours)))
```

## Numeric transformations

Transformation functions return a vector **the same length as the input**: a natural fit for `mutate()`.

You can use `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, and `^` on vectors. When two vectors have different lengths, R **recycles** the shorter one by repeating it until it matches the longer one.

```{webr}
x <- c(1, 2, 10, 20)
x / 5
# is shorthand for
x / c(5, 5, 5, 5)
```

## A silent recycling bug in `filter()`

Recycling also works with comparisons, which can quietly give wrong answers. Students in Arts or Business?

```{webr}
survey |>
  filter(program == c("Arts", "Business")) |>
  count(program)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="No error, wrong answer"}
R compares `program` with `"Arts", "Business", "Arts", "Business", ...` row by row. It does **not** ask "is the program Arts or Business?". You only get about half of the students.
:::

The fix is `%in%`, which you met last lecture:

```{webr}
survey |>
  filter(program %in% c("Arts", "Business")) |>
  count(program)
```

## Minimum and maximum: `pmin()` and `pmax()`

Two kinds of min and max exist:

- `pmin()` and `pmax()` work **row by row** across vectors (the "p" is for parallel)
- `min()` and `max()` summarize **everything** into one value

```{webr}
df <- tribble(
  ~x, ~y,
  1,  3,
  5,  2,
  7, NA,
)

df |>
  mutate(
    min = pmin(x, y, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = pmax(x, y, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

## The summary versions

```{webr}
df <- tribble(
  ~x, ~y,
  1,  3,
  5,  2,
  7, NA,
)

df |>
  mutate(
    min = min(x, y, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(x, y, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

::: {.callout-important title="Key idea"}
Every row gets the **same** answer from `min()` and `max()`: the smallest and largest value in both columns combined. Use `pmin()` and `pmax()` for a per-row answer.
:::

## `pmax()` on the survey

Which is each student's heavier weekly commitment: studying or working?

```{webr}
survey |>
  mutate(
    heavier = pmax(study_hours_week, work_hours_week),
    .keep = "used"
  )
```

## Modular arithmetic

Modular arithmetic is division with a quotient and a remainder:

- `%/%` is **integer division** (how many whole times it fits)
- `%%` is the **remainder**

```{webr}
1:10 %/% 3
1:10 %% 3
```

## Hours and minutes

`sleep_hours = 6.7` means 6 hours and 42 minutes. Modular arithmetic splits it:

```{webr}
survey |>
  mutate(
    hours = sleep_hours %/% 1,
    minutes = round((sleep_hours %% 1) * 60),
    .keep = "used"
  )
```

- `%/% 1` keeps the whole hours
- `%% 1` keeps the fraction, and `* 60` turns it into minutes

## Rounding

`round(x)` rounds to the nearest integer. The `digits` argument controls where to round, and it can be **negative**.

```{webr}
round(123.456)
round(123.456, 2)   # two digits
round(123.456, 1)   # one digit
round(123.456, -1)  # round to the nearest ten
round(123.456, -2)  # round to the nearest hundred
```

Grades rounded to the nearest ten:

```{webr}
survey |>
  count(grade_tens = round(avg_grade, -1))
```

## `floor()` and `ceiling()`

- `floor()` always rounds **down**
- `ceiling()` always rounds **up**
- Neither has a `digits` argument, so you scale first

```{webr}
x <- 123.456

floor(x)
ceiling(x)

# Round down to the nearest two digits
floor(x / 0.01) * 0.01
# Round up to the nearest two digits
ceiling(x / 0.01) * 0.01
```

## Cutting numbers into ranges

`cut()` chops a numeric vector into **bins** and returns a factor. You supply the break points.

```{webr}
x <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20)
cut(x, breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20))
```

Give `labels` one **fewer** element than `breaks`, because there is one fewer bin than break points:

```{webr}
x <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20)
cut(x,
  breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20),
  labels = c("sm", "md", "lg", "xl")
)
```

## Values outside the breaks

Anything outside the breaks becomes `NA`:

```{webr}
y <- c(NA, -10, 5, 10, 30)
cut(y, breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20))
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Open-ended bins"}
Use `-Inf` and `Inf` as the outer breaks so nothing falls off the ends. Bins are right-closed by default, like `(5, 10]`. Pass `right = FALSE` to make them left-closed, like `[5, 10)`.
:::

## `cut()` on the survey

Lecture 8 made sleep groups with `case_when()`. `cut()` does the same job in one line:

```{webr}
survey |>
  mutate(
    sleep_group = cut(
      sleep_hours,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 6, 7.5, Inf),
      labels = c("Short", "Typical", "Long"),
      right = FALSE
    ),
    .keep = "used"
  ) |>
  count(sleep_group)
```

::: {.callout-caution title="Boundaries differ"}
With `right = FALSE` a student at exactly 7.5 hours lands in **Long**. Lecture 8's `case_when()` put them in **Typical**. Always check what happens at the boundaries.
:::

## Ranking

`min_rank()` gives the rank of each value. `1` is the smallest, unless you flip it with `desc()`.

```{webr}
survey |>
  group_by(program) |>
  summarize(mean_sleep = mean(sleep_hours, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(
    rank_least = min_rank(mean_sleep),
    rank_most = min_rank(desc(mean_sleep))
  )
```

- Which program sleeps the least?
- Other ranking functions are in the appendix

## Summaries: mean or median?

```{webr}
survey |>
  summarize(
    mean_work = mean(work_hours_week),
    median_work = median(work_hours_week)
  )
```

Why are they so different? Look at the distribution:

```{webr}
ggplot(survey, aes(x = work_hours_week)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Key idea"}
Many students do not work at all, which drags the median down while a few heavy workers pull the mean up. When a distribution is **skewed**, report the median, or report both.
:::

## Spread

How much do students *within* a program differ?

```{webr}
survey |>
  group_by(program) |>
  summarize(
    sd_sleep = sd(sleep_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    iqr_sleep = IQR(sleep_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_sleep = min(sleep_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_sleep = max(sleep_hours, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

- `sd()` is the standard deviation, `IQR()` is the width of the middle half of the data
- `IQR()` is less affected by extreme values

## Putting Part 1 together

```{webr}
program_summary <- survey |>
  filter(!is.na(sleep_hours)) |>
  group_by(program) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean_sleep = mean(sleep_hours)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    hours = mean_sleep %/% 1,
    minutes = round((mean_sleep %% 1) * 60),
    rank_least = min_rank(mean_sleep)
  )

program_summary
```

::: {.callout-caution title="Run this one first"}
Parts 2 and 3 reuse `program_summary`. If a later cell complains it cannot find it, run this cell again.
:::

# Part 2: Strings

::: {.notes}
~25 min including Exercise 2. The book's order is slightly different: we follow the story instead.
:::

## When do students go to bed?

Strings (text) are everywhere in real data. Our survey has a `bedtime` column that students **typed in themselves**.

| Step | Tool (Chapter 14) |
|------|-------------------|
| Build labels from data | `str_c()`, `str_glue()`, `str_flatten()` |
| Measure and slice text | `str_length()`, `str_sub()` |
| Split one column into several | `separate_wider_delim()` |
| Tidy up capitals | `str_to_lower()` |

::: {.callout-note title="Coming next"}
The most powerful string tool, **regular expressions**, is the topic of Lecture 10. Today we see how far the basic tools get us.
:::

## Combining fixed text with data

`str_c()` takes any number of vectors and returns a character vector. It is similar to base R's `paste0()`, but it follows tidyverse recycling rules.

```{webr}
str_c("x", "y", "z")
str_c("Hello ", c("John", "Susan"))
```

Inside `mutate()`:

```{webr}
df <- tibble(name = c("Flora", "David", "Terra", NA))
df |> mutate(greeting = str_c("Hi ", name, "!"))
```

::: {.callout-important title="Missing values are contagious"}
Just like in arithmetic, if any input is `NA`, the result is `NA`. The fourth greeting is missing.
:::

## `str_glue()`

`str_c()` gets awkward with many pieces. `str_glue()` lets you write the whole string in one go, with `{ }` marking code to evaluate.

```{webr}
df <- tibble(name = c("Flora", "David", "Terra", NA))
df |> mutate(greeting = str_glue("Hi {name}!"))
```

::: {.callout-warning title="NA behaves differently"}
Unlike `str_c()`, `str_glue()` converts a missing value to the **text** `"NA"`.
:::

## Labels for our chart

Using the `program_summary` from Part 1:

```{webr}
program_summary |>
  mutate(label = str_glue("{program}: {hours} h {minutes} min"))
```

- This is the label we used on the first slide

## `str_flatten()`

`str_c()` and `str_glue()` return **one result per input**. `str_flatten()` goes the other way: it collapses a vector into a **single** string. That makes it a summary function.

```{webr}
str_flatten(c("x", "y", "z"))
str_flatten(c("x", "y", "z"), ", ")
str_flatten(c("x", "y", "z"), ", ", last = ", and ")
```

## `str_flatten()` by group

Which drinks does each program prefer? List the distinct ones:

```{webr}
survey |>
  group_by(program) |>
  summarize(
    drinks = str_flatten(sort(unique(favourite_drink)), ", ", last = ", and ")
  )
```

::: {.callout-note title="Why sort()?"}
`sort()` drops the `NA`s and puts the drinks in alphabetical order.
:::

## Now the real problem: `bedtime`

```{webr}
survey |>
  select(student_id, bedtime) |>
  head(15)
```

How many different ways did students write their bedtime?

```{webr}
survey |>
  summarize(distinct_bedtimes = n_distinct(bedtime))
```

## The same time, written many ways

```{webr}
survey |>
  count(bedtime, sort = TRUE)
```

- `11:30 PM`, `11:30 pm`, `11.30 pm`, `23:30`, `2330`...
- Some entries are not times at all
- We need to **clean** this column before we can use it

## Looking at the length: `str_length()`

`str_length()` counts the characters in each string. A missing value gives `NA`.

```{webr}
str_length(c("a", "R for data science", NA))
```

On the survey:

```{webr}
survey |>
  count(length = str_length(bedtime))
```

## The long ones

```{webr}
survey |>
  filter(str_length(bedtime) > 10) |>
  count(bedtime, sort = TRUE)
```

- Long entries are usually hedged answers (`around ...`) or words instead of times
- A computer cannot turn these into times without extra rules

## Splitting `bedtime` into columns

A time like `"11:30 pm"` has two pieces separated by a space. tidyr's `separate_wider_delim()` splits a column on a delimiter, with a new column per piece. You must supply **names** for the new columns.

```{webr}
df3 <- tibble(x = c("a10.1.2022", "b10.2.2011", "e15.1.2015"))

df3 |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    x,
    delim = ".",
    names = c("code", "edition", "year")
  )
```

## Let's try it on `bedtime`

```{webr}
#| error: true
survey |>
  select(student_id, bedtime) |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    bedtime,
    delim = " ",
    names = c("time", "ampm")
  )
```

::: {.callout-warning title="It refuses to guess"}
`separate_wider_delim()` expects every string to split into the **same number** of pieces. Real data does not. The function **errors** rather than guessing, and the message tells you what to try.
:::

## Debug mode

`too_few = "debug"` and `too_many = "debug"` keep the result but add diagnostic columns, named after the input column:

- `bedtime_ok`: did this row split cleanly?
- `bedtime_pieces`: how many pieces it had
- `bedtime_remainder`: any leftover text

```{webr}
bed_debug <- survey |>
  select(student_id, bedtime) |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    bedtime,
    delim = " ",
    names = c("time", "ampm"),
    too_few = "debug",
    too_many = "debug"
  )

bed_debug |>
  count(bedtime_ok, bedtime_pieces)
```

## Which rows failed?

```{webr}
bed_debug <- survey |>
  select(student_id, bedtime) |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    bedtime,
    delim = " ",
    names = c("time", "ampm"),
    too_few = "debug",
    too_many = "debug"
  )

bed_debug |>
  filter(!bedtime_ok) |>
  count(bedtime, bedtime_pieces, sort = TRUE)
```

- **Too few** pieces: `11:30PM`, `2330`, `midnight`
- **Too many** pieces: `around 11 pm`, `no set time`, and entries with a stray space at the start

## Fixing it: tidy first

Two easy fixes before splitting:

- `str_trim()` removes stray spaces at the start and end
- `str_to_lower()` makes `PM`, `Pm` and `pm` the same

```{webr}
survey |>
  mutate(bedtime_clean = str_to_lower(str_trim(bedtime))) |>
  summarize(
    before = n_distinct(bedtime),
    after = n_distinct(bedtime_clean)
  )
```

## Fixing it: tell the function what to do

Once you understand the problem, tell the function what to do:

- `too_few = "align_start"` fills missing pieces with `NA` at the **end**
- `too_many = "merge"` glues the extra pieces onto the **last** column

```{webr}
bed_clean <- survey |>
  select(student_id, bedtime) |>
  mutate(bedtime = str_to_lower(str_trim(bedtime))) |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    bedtime,
    delim = " ",
    names = c("time", "ampm"),
    too_few = "align_start",
    too_many = "merge"
  )

bed_clean |>
  count(ampm, sort = TRUE)
```

## A shortcut: `str_sub()`

`str_sub(string, start, end)` extracts part of each string. Both `start` and `end` are **inclusive**. Negative positions count from the **end**.

```{webr}
x <- c("Apple", "Banana", "Pear")
str_sub(x, 1, 3)
str_sub(x, -3, -1)
```

`str_sub()` does not fail if the string is too short:

```{webr}
str_sub("a", 1, 5)
```

## The last two letters of `bedtime`

Most entries end in `am` or `pm`, even when the spacing is inconsistent:

```{webr}
survey |>
  mutate(last2 = str_sub(str_to_lower(str_trim(bedtime)), -2, -1)) |>
  count(last2, sort = TRUE)
```

- Most rows are `am` or `pm`
- `30`, `00`, and similar values are 24-hour times
- The rest are words and other leftovers

## Back to logical vectors

Lecture 8 tools turn those two letters into a clean label:

```{webr}
survey |>
  mutate(
    last2 = str_sub(str_to_lower(str_trim(bedtime)), -2, -1),
    ampm = case_when(
      last2 == "am" ~ "AM",
      last2 == "pm" ~ "PM"
    )
  ) |>
  count(ampm)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Notice what is still NA"}
Blank answers, 24-hour times, and words like `midnight` all end up as `NA`. We have not **solved** the column, only made a start.
:::

## How far did we get?

| Problem | Solved today? |
|---------|---------------|
| Capital letters (`PM`, `Pm`, `pm`) | Yes: `str_to_lower()` |
| Stray spaces | Yes: `str_trim()` |
| AM or PM at the end | Mostly: `str_sub()` (but `p.m.` ends in `m.`) |
| Pulling out the hour and minute when separators differ (`11:30pm`, `11.30 pm`, `1130`) | **No** |
| Hedged answers (`around 11`, `~11:30 pm`) | **No** |
| 24-hour (`23:30`, `2330`) and no AM/PM (`11:30`) | **No** |
| `midnight`, `idk` | **No** |

::: {.callout-note title="Next lecture"}
We need a way to describe a **pattern** instead of an exact string. That is what regular expressions do (Chapter 15).
:::

2. Create `ampm`: the last two characters of the trimmed, lower-case `bedtime`. Count the values. Which ones are **not** `am` or `pm`?

  filter(str_length(bedtime) > 10) |>

# Part 3: Factors

::: {.notes}
~20 min including Exercise 3.
:::

## Can we make the chart readable?

Back to our dean's chart. Here is what the pipeline gives us **without** any work:

```{webr}
program_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_sleep, y = program)) +
  geom_point(size = 3)
```

- Programs are in **alphabetical** order, which tells the dean nothing
- Categorical variables that need a **specific order** are what factors are for

## Why factors?

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
A **factor** is how R stores a categorical variable that has a fixed set of possible values, called **levels**.
:::

Strings sort alphabetically, which is rarely what you want:

```{webr}
x1 <- c("Dec", "Apr", "Jan", "Mar")
sort(x1)
```

## Creating a factor

Start with a list of valid levels, then pass it to `factor()`:

```{webr}
month_levels <- c(
  "Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
  "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"
)

x1 <- c("Dec", "Apr", "Jan", "Mar")
y1 <- factor(x1, levels = month_levels)

y1
sort(y1)
levels(y1)
```

## Typos become `NA`

```{webr}
x2 <- c("Dec", "Apr", "Jam", "Mar")
factor(x2, levels = month_levels)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Silent NA"}
Any value that is **not** in `levels` silently becomes `NA`. There is no warning. Always check the result.
:::

## Reordering levels: `fct_reorder()`

`fct_reorder(f, x)` orders the levels of `f` by the values in `x`. It is perfect for plots:

```{webr}
program_summary |>
  mutate(program = fct_reorder(program, mean_sleep)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_sleep, y = program)) +
  geom_point(size = 3)
```

- The program that sleeps the least is at the bottom, the most at the top

## Reordering by hand: `fct_relevel()`

Sleep groups from Lecture 8 are **text**, so a plot puts them in alphabetical order:

```{webr}
survey |>
  filter(!is.na(sleep_hours)) |>
  mutate(
    sleep_group = case_when(
      sleep_hours < 6    ~ "Short",
      sleep_hours <= 7.5 ~ "Typical",
      sleep_hours > 7.5  ~ "Long"
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sleep_group)) +
  geom_bar()
```

## Fixing the order

`fct_relevel()` lets you list the levels in the order you want:

```{webr}
survey |>
  filter(!is.na(sleep_hours)) |>
  mutate(
    sleep_group = case_when(
      sleep_hours < 6    ~ "Short",
      sleep_hours <= 7.5 ~ "Typical",
      sleep_hours > 7.5  ~ "Long"
    ),
    sleep_group = fct_relevel(sleep_group, "Short", "Typical", "Long")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sleep_group)) +
  geom_bar()
```

- This replaces the `scale_x_discrete(limits = ...)` trick from Lecture 8

## Order by frequency: `fct_infreq()`

For bar charts, ordering by how common each level is usually helps:

```{webr}
survey |>
  filter(!is.na(favourite_drink)) |>
  mutate(favourite_drink = fct_infreq(favourite_drink)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = favourite_drink)) +
  geom_bar()
```

## Changing level **values**

Sometimes the problem is not the order, but the levels themselves:

- `fct_recode()` renames levels
- `fct_collapse()` merges several levels into one group
- `fct_lump_n()` combines the rare levels into `"Other"`

## `fct_recode()`

```{webr}
survey |>
  filter(!is.na(favourite_drink)) |>
  mutate(drink = fct_recode(favourite_drink, "Soda" = "Pop")) |>
  count(drink)
```

- The syntax is `new name = "old name"`
- Levels you do not mention stay the same

::: {.callout-caution title="Typos in old names"}
If you misspell an old level, `fct_recode()` leaves things unchanged. Check the counts after you recode.
:::

## `fct_collapse()`

Group the drinks by how much caffeine they usually contain:

```{webr}
survey |>
  filter(!is.na(favourite_drink)) |>
  mutate(
    caffeine = fct_collapse(
      favourite_drink,
      Strong = c("Coffee", "Energy drink"),
      Mild = c("Tea", "Pop"),
      None = "Water"
    )
  ) |>
  count(caffeine)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="A lookup table is better"}
Typing groupings by hand is fine for five drinks. With many levels, you would use a lookup table with the caffeine amounts instead. That is a **join**, in Lecture 11.
:::

## `fct_lump_n()`

Combine the smallest levels into `"Other"`. Keep the top `n`:

```{webr}
survey |>
  filter(!is.na(favourite_drink)) |>
  mutate(drink = fct_lump_n(favourite_drink, n = 2)) |>
  count(drink, sort = TRUE)
```

- Other versions: `fct_lump_min()`, `fct_lump_prop()`

## The finished chart

```{webr}
program_summary |>
  mutate(
    program = fct_reorder(program, mean_sleep),
    label = str_glue("{hours} h {minutes} min")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_sleep, y = program)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), nudge_y = 0.3) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(5, 8)) +
  labs(
    title = "Average sleep by program",
    x = "Hours per night", y = NULL
  )
```

- **Numbers** gave us the averages, the hours and minutes
- **Strings** gave us the label
- **Factors** gave us the order

## Exercise 3

::: {.callout-tip title="Live exercise"}
Make a bar chart of `favourite_drink` for students who answered the question:

1. Order the bars from the most common drink to the least common
2. Keep the top 3 drinks and lump the rest into `"Other"`
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_factors
survey |>
  filter(!is.na(favourite_drink)) |>
  mutate(
    favourite_drink =
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = favourite_drink)) +
  geom_bar()
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_factors
#| solution: true
survey |>
  filter(!is.na(favourite_drink)) |>
  mutate(
    favourite_drink = fct_infreq(favourite_drink),
    favourite_drink = fct_lump_n(favourite_drink, n = 3)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = favourite_drink)) +
  geom_bar()
```

## Numbers: other tools {.smaller}

| Tool | What it does | Tiny example | Read the section on |
|------|--------------|--------------|---------------------|
| `parse_double()` | Turns clean text into numbers | `parse_double("1.2")` | Making numbers |
| `log()`, `log2()`, `log10()` | Logarithms. Each +1 on `log2()` means the value **doubled** | `log2(c(1, 2, 4, 8))` | Logarithms |
| `floor()`, `ceiling()` | Round down / up. No `digits` argument, so scale first | `floor(123.456)` | Rounding |
| `cumsum()`, `cummean()`, ... | Running totals, means, minimums, maximums | `cumsum(1:10)` | Cumulative aggregates |
| `lag()`, `lead()` | The previous / next value, for comparing neighbours | `x - lag(x)` | Offsets |
| `consecutive_id()` | Starts a new id every time a value changes | `consecutive_id(c(1, 1, 2, 2, 1))` | Consecutive identifiers |
| `dense_rank()`, `row_number()`, `percent_rank()` | Other ways to rank, with different tie handling | `row_number(x)` | Ranks |
| `quantile()` | Any percentile of a vector | `quantile(x, 0.9)` | Minimum, maximum, and quantiles |
| `first()`, `last()`, `nth()` | Pick a value by position | `first(x)` | Positions |
| `cut_interval()`, `cut_number()`, `cut_width()` | ggplot2 helpers for common binning patterns | `cut_width(x, 10)` | Cutting numbers into ranges |

## Strings: other tools {.smaller}

| Tool | What it does | Tiny example | Read the section on |
|------|--------------|--------------|---------------------|
| Escapes: `\"`, `\\` | Put a quote or backslash **inside** a string | `"He said \"hi\""` | Escapes |
| Raw strings: `r"(...)"` | Write a string without escaping anything | `r"(C:\data)"` | Raw strings |
| `\n`, `\t`, `\u00b5` | New line, tab, and other special characters | `"a\tb"` | Other special characters |
| `str_view()` | Shows the **raw** contents of a string, without the escapes | `str_view("a\\b")` | Escapes |

| `separate_longer_delim()`, `separate_longer_position()` | Split into **rows** instead of columns | `separate_longer_delim(x, ",")` | Separating into rows |
| `separate_wider_position()` | Split fixed-width text into columns | `widths = c(year = 4, age = 2)` | Separating into columns |
| `too_few` / `too_many` options | `"drop"`, `"merge"`, `"align_start"`, `"align_end"` | `too_many = "drop"` | Diagnosing widening problems |
| `str_to_upper()`, `str_to_title()` | Change capitals | `str_to_title("jane doe")` | Non-English text |
